title: Do our models capture the range of ENSO events?
abstract: An event-based space–time analog approach is described for diagnosing ENSO mechanisms and variability in coupled models, specifically to evaluate whether these models capture the full range of ENSO variability through direct comparisons with observed events. In this analog approach, model states were drawn from an extensive library of states previously simulated in multi-century present-day simulations using the Community Earth System Model (CESM1) and the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM1) at both ocean eddy-parameterized (~ 1°) and ocean eddy-resolving (~ 0.1°) scales by matching their sea surface temperature (SST) and sea surface height (SSH) components to observed initial tropical Indo-Pacific SST and SSH anomalies. The subsequent space–time evolution of these states over the next several months in the simulations is evaluated for capturing selected ENSO events. The results indicate that neither model shows significant improvements in mean-state biases when the resolution is increased. In contrast to their biases, the low-resolution E3SM1-LR and CESM1-LR models consistently outperform their higher-resolution counterparts in all Eastern and Central Pacific warm events, as well as in cold events for SST and SSH-based analogs. However, RMSE values for SSH-based analogs display errors about twice as large as those of SST-based, which ramp up quickly with the analog ranking. The analog approach successfully captures the observed space–time evolution and peak characteristics of strong Eastern and Central Pacific warm and cold events. Nevertheless, all models display excessive variability in the western-central Pacific during both warm and cold events and struggle to accurately reproduce the magnitude of anomalies near the eastern boundary. Furthermore, the stronger the event, the more effective the analogs are, with only modest differences related to resolution, as low-resolution SST-based analogs consistently outperform their high-resolution counterparts.
problem: Current climate models are challenged in their ability to capture the full range of observed ENSO variability, often exhibiting excessive variability in the western-central Pacific and struggling to reproduce the magnitude of anomalies near the eastern boundary.
method: This paper describes an event-based space-time analog approach to evaluate whether coupled models capture the full range of ENSO variability by matching the space-time evolution of simulated sea surface temperature and height anomalies with observed events from a library of multi-century simulations.
task: The task is to evaluate whether coupled climate models capture the full range of ENSO variability by comparing model simulations to observed events using an event-based space-time analog approach.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: However, the impact of climate model resolution on ENSO simulations is yet to be fully understood, with recent studies using the Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 1 (E3SMv1) showing that increasing ocean horizontal resolution does not lead to fundamental improvements in ENSO simulations (Caldwell et al. 2019), while others found improvements in some ENSO-related characteristics and teleconnections (Kirtman et al. 2012; Small et al. 2014; Prodhomme et al. 2016). In the tropical Pacific, eddy-driven heat flux, which is not explicitly resolved in models with coarse horizontal resolution, is assumed to increase during La Niña and decrease during El Niño, constraining ENSO amplitude and contributing to ENSO asymmetry (An 2008; Graham 2014).

An example of model bias in SST and momentum flux is illustrated in Fig. 1. The E3SM1 model exhibits a cold tongue that is excessively cold in the central-eastern Pacific and extends too far westward, accompanied by a consistent wind stress bias, which is excessively easterly during both the June-July-August (JJA) and December-January-February (DJF) seasons. The cold tongue bias is most pronounced in the eastern Pacific during JJA but weakens and shifts toward the central Pacific in DJF, except for CESM1-HR (Fig. 1f).

In contrast, the CESM1 model exhibits more pronounced seasonality in its bias and even more marked sensitivity to resolution, where the low-resolution model bias is ubiquitously warmer than that of the high-resolution model. Overall, the cold tongue bias in CESM1 is less severe, demonstrating only a mild cold bias in the central Pacific, except during the DJF season for the high-resolution model.
